analysis.one_liner: Cuts campaign ad and postage costs for House candidates who accept spending limits and tightens rules on PAC, big-donor, and bundler money.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to three House committees and two subcommittees in June 1997, it never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill offered House candidates a deal: accept a $600,000 campaign spending cap (adjustable for inflation), rely mostly on small and in-state contributions, and limit your own personal spending, and in exchange you get broadcast ads at half the lowest station rate and reduced postage [S2][S3]. It also capped how much PAC money and large individual contributions any House candidate could take, banned the 'leadership PACs' lawmakers use to spread money to colleagues, required lobbyists and bundlers to disclose the money they deliver, barred contributions from people who cannot vote in federal elections, and closed loopholes that let outside groups coordinate secretly with campaigns [S2][S3]. The idea was to make it possible to win a House seat without depending on special-interest money, and to make whatever money flows more visible [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: House challengers and candidates without deep pockets or PAC connections, who could run competitive campaigns on a spending cap with half-price advertising and cheap mail; voters in districts where candidates must draw most small donations from within their own state; and the public interest in knowing who is bundling money to which lawmakers.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who agree to a $600,000 spending cap, a 60% in-state small-donor requirement, and tight personal-fund limits get television and radio ads at 50% of the station's lowest charge plus reduced postal rates [S2][S3].

PAC contributions to House candidates would be capped at 25% of the applicable spending limit, and large individual contributions (over $250) would be capped in the aggregate for House candidates [S2][S3].

The bill prohibits 'leadership committees' — political committees that sitting federal officeholders set up and control outside their own campaign — forcing existing ones to disburse their funds within a year [S3].
Bundlers, including lobbyists, would have their delivered contributions counted and reported as coming through them, so candidates could not hide who routed money to them [S3].

It redefines 'express advocacy' and treats payments coordinated with a campaign as contributions, closing the loophole where outside groups run ads in coordination with a candidate while claiming independence [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadcast and cable companies, which would have to sell ad time to complying candidates at half price and give up discretion over preempting those ads; PACs, large individual donors, lobbyists who bundle contributions; and members of Congress whose leadership PACs would be shut down.

drawbacks.text: The spending cap could hurt candidates in expensive media markets, where $600,000 buys little airtime, and the bill's response — raising the cap when a wealthy self-funded opponent spends more — creates complicated triggers that critics could call unworkable [S3].

Forcing broadcasters to sell ads at half price is effectively taking property; the bill itself acknowledges this by routing constitutional challenges to those rates to the Court of Federal Claims with money damages as the only remedy [S3].

The expanded definition of 'express advocacy' reaches a wide range of political communications, which raises First Act concerns about restricting political speech that courts at the time (under Buckley v. Valeo) treated as protected — a serious constitutional risk even supporters had to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain — cheap ads and postage in exchange for spending limits and a small-donor base — is a straightforward way to reduce candidates' dependence on PAC and large-donor money, and the bundler and coordination rules address real loopholes in the law. The costs fall on broadcasters (a discounted mandate with acknowledged takings risk) and on the ability of wealthy candidates and big-money groups to dominate House races, which was the point. The main honest criticism is design: the escalating limits and triggers are complex, and some provisions would likely have faced serious constitutional challenge — which the bill tried to preempt with expedited Supreme Court review [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees two weeks later, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Meehan introduced the bill on June 4, 1997 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Oversight, Commerce, and Government Reform committees, with the Speaker to later decide how jurisdiction was split [S5].
On June 16 and June 18, 1997, it was referred to the Government Management subcommittee and the Telecommunications subcommittee, respectively [S5].
No hearings, markups, or floor action followed, and the bill expired with the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbents who rely on PAC and leadership-PAC money, big donors and lobbying bundlers, and broadcasters selling full-price political ads are better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Martin T. Meehan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 13 of 226 House Republicans
for.role: Republican cosponsors, including Reps. Shays, Leach, and Castle

against.name: House Oversight Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: House Commerce and Government Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees in June 1997 and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to three committees at once with jurisdiction 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker,' a referral pattern that splits a bill among committees and makes floor action unlikely.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but uneven: the sponsor was a Democrat and 13 of the 20 cosponsors were Republicans, yet the bill died in subcommittee without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill required stations to sell ad time to complying House candidates at 50% of their lowest rate, limited their ability to preempt candidate ads, and conditioned license renewal on compliance. Stations' existing revenue from selling political ads at full price during campaigns would be reduced.
The bill extended license revocation to cable systems that refused candidates reasonable access, requiring them to sell airtime to candidates on the same terms as their most favored advertiser.

industries.industry: Political action committees and large donors
industries.note: PAC money would be capped at 25% of a House campaign's spending limit, large individual contributions would face aggregate caps, and the ability of outside interests to fund a House candidate's air war would shrink.

Contributions delivered by bundlers, including registered lobbyists, would be attributed to and reported through the bundler, reducing the value of fundraising relationships that don't appear on the record.

The bill bans political committees that sitting federal officeholders establish and control outside their own campaigns, and requires existing ones to disburse their funds within a year — eliminating a channel members use to collect and re-distribute special-interest money.
